vignette:
After several sessions, Mrs. Anowa has begun to share the story of what happened. She speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, the same rhythm she once used to brief ministry officials on complex policy proposals. Now, however, her words carry a weight that settles in the room long after she has finished speaking.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in late November, two years ago. She had just left a meeting at the Ministry of Finance, where she had presented a 50-page analysis on urban housing subsidies—a document she had spent months refining. At eighty, she had no intention of retiring. Her mind was still sharp, her opinions still sought after. She drove her old sedan, the same one her late husband had bought in 1995, along the highway toward her apartment in the eastern suburbs. The rain had started suddenly, a violent West African downpour that turned the asphalt into a mirror of grey sky. She slowed down, gripping the wheel with both hands, her knuckles pale.

The lorry came from her left, running a red light at the intersection. She remembers the sound—a deep, metallic groan mixed with the shattering of glass. Then nothing. She woke up in the hospital three days later, her right leg in traction, four ribs cracked, a deep gash across her forehead. The doctors said she was lucky. The lorry had crushed the driver’s side door, but the old sedan’s frame had held. She should have died.

Now, two years later, Mrs. Anowa no longer drives. She cannot even sit in the passenger seat of a car without feeling her chest tighten. The first time her daughter tried to take her to the market, she began hyperventilating before they had left the driveway. Her daughter turned back, frustrated and frightened. Mrs. Anowa now takes taxis only when absolutely necessary, and only if she sits in the back seat behind the driver, where she can see both side mirrors. She grips the door handle the entire ride, her eyes fixed on the road ahead, counting the seconds until she can step out onto solid ground.

Her work has suffered. As a policy analyst, she used to thrive on field visits—travelling to rural districts to interview community leaders, assess infrastructure needs, gather data. Now she refuses all assignments that require travel. Her supervisor has been patient, but the team has begun to assign her only desk-based tasks. She spends long hours alone in her office, staring at the same paragraph on a report without reading it. Her mind drifts to the sound of crunching metal, the smell of gasoline and wet earth. She has stopped taking public transport altogether; the honking of buses triggers a cold sweat.

At night, she sleeps in the armchair in her living room, the television on low. The bedroom reminds her of the hospital bed. She dreams of the collision—not the impact, but the moments before it, the headlights of the lorry growing larger, the rain on the windshield. She wakes up gasping, her hands reaching for a steering wheel that isn’t there. She no longer calls her daughter, because she doesn’t want to worry her. Instead, she sits in the dark, repeating the breathing exercises the physiotherapist taught her for the ribs.

She has not told anyone about the sudden, sharp rages that overtake her when she hears a car horn or sees a truck in her peripheral vision. She has not told anyone that she sometimes wishes she had died in the crash, because then she would not have to live with this constant vigilance, this sense that every intersection is a potential end. She has not told anyone that she misses the woman she used to be—the one who drove confidently through city traffic, who argued with taxi drivers, who traveled to remote villages without a second thought.

Yesterday, during our session, she said quietly, “I used to think policy was about controlling the future. Now I know that nothing is under control. A red light means nothing.” She looked down at her hands, the same hands that once typed lengthy reports, now trembling slightly on her lap. She has not touched her policy briefs in three weeks.
